title: Minimum Wage and Employment: A Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Main Analysis
To replicate the main idea, I compare employment levels in New Jersey and Pennsylvania before and after the policy change.
The main method used in this paper is difference-in-differences. First, I calculate how employment changed over time within each state. Then I compare those changes across the two states. This helps control for overall trends that might affect both states.
From my replication, I find that employment in New Jersey does not decrease relative to Pennsylvania after the minimum wage increase. This is consistent with the original paper’s conclusion, which suggests that the effect of minimum wage on employment is not as negative as we might expect.

title: Minimum Wage and Employment: A Replication of Card and Krueger (1994)
text:
Something Additional
As an additional step, I compared the average employment levels for both states before and after the policy change.
Looking at the data, the trends in New Jersey and Pennsylvania are quite similar. There is no clear drop in employment in New Jersey after the minimum wage increase. This makes the result easier to understand beyond just the numerical estimates.
Overall, this comparison supports the idea that the minimum wage increase did not lead to a noticeable decrease in employment in this case.

text:
Card and Krueger (1994) study whether an increase in the minimum wage reduced employment in the fast-food industry. In April 1992, New Jersey raised its minimum wage from $4.25 to $5.05 per hour, while neighboring Pennsylvania did not. This policy change creates a natural comparison between treated stores in New Jersey and control stores in Pennsylvania.
The paper uses a difference-in-differences design. The basic idea is to compare employment changes in New Jersey before and after the policy to employment changes in Pennsylvania over the same period. If employment trends would have moved similarly in the two states without the policy change, then the difference in these changes can be interpreted as the causal effect of the minimum wage increase.
In this post, I replicate key findings from Card and Krueger (1994), focusing on the sample structure and the first three rows and first three columns of Table 3.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Suppose I manage a website with a landing page that invites visitors to sign up for a newsletter. I want to know whether the wording of the call to action affects whether visitors subscribe. In this experiment, CTA A says “Sign up for our newsletter here!” while CTA B says “Stay up to date by signing up!” Visitors are randomly assigned to see one of the two versions, and I compare the sign-up rates between the groups.
This is a standard A/B test. The goal is to estimate whether one version of the message leads to a higher conversion rate than the other. More broadly, this example provides a useful setting for understanding several key ideas in frequentist statistics, including simulation, the law of large numbers, the bootstrap, hypothesis testing, and the risks of repeated peeking at the data.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Suppose I manage a website with a landing page that invites visitors to sign up for a newsletter. I want to know whether the wording of the call to action affects whether visitors subscribe. In this experiment, CTA A says “Sign up for our newsletter here!” while CTA B says “Stay up to date by signing up!” Visitors are randomly assigned to see one of the two versions, and I compare the sign-up rates between the groups.
This is a standard A/B test. The goal is to estimate whether one version of the message leads to a higher conversion rate than the other. More broadly, this example provides a useful setting for understanding several key ideas in frequentist statistics, including simulation, the law of large numbers, the bootstrap, hypothesis testing, and the risks of repeated peeking at the data.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
section: The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
text:
The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
Each visitor either signs up for the newsletter or does not, so the outcome for each person is binary. Because of this, each observation can be modeled as a Bernoulli random variable with a success probability equal to the probability of signing up.
Let \(\pi_A\) represent the probability of signing up under CTA A, and let \(\pi_B\) represent the probability of signing up under CTA B. The main parameter of interest is the difference in conversion rates:
\[
\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B
\]
In the sample, I estimate this quantity using the difference in observed sign-up proportions:
\[
\hat{\theta} = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B
\]
Since the outcome is either 0 or 1, the sample mean in each group is just the proportion of visitors who signed up. This makes the difference in sample means a natural estimator for the treatment effect in this A/B test.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Simulating Data
In a real A/B test, the true conversion rates would be unknown. However, simulation is useful because it allows me to study how the estimator behaves when the true values are known. For this exercise, I assume that the sign-up probability under CTA A is \(\pi_A = 0.22\) and the sign-up probability under CTA B is \(\pi_B = 0.18\). This means the true treatment effect is:
\[
\theta = 0.22 - 0.18 = 0.04
\]
Using these values, I simulate 1,000 visitors in each group and compare the observed conversion rates.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

np.random.seed(42)

pi_A = 0.22
pi_B = 0.18
n = 1000

A = np.random.binomial(1, pi_A, n)
B = np.random.binomial(1, pi_B, n)

theta_hat = A.mean() - B.mean()

summary_df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Group": ["CTA A", "CTA B"],
    "Signup Rate": [A.mean(), B.mean()]

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Law of Large Numbers
The Law of Large Numbers says that as the sample size grows, the sample average gets closer to the true population average. In this A/B test, that means the estimated treatment effect should move closer to the true difference in conversion rates as more observations are included. With only a few observations, the estimate can fluctuate a lot, but with a larger sample it becomes more stable.
To illustrate this, I compute the element-wise differences between the simulated outcomes in group A and group B, then calculate the cumulative average of those differences. If the Law of Large Numbers is working as expected, the running mean should gradually settle near the true treatment effect of 0.04.

diffs = A - B
running_mean = np.cumsum(diffs) / np.arange(1, n + 1)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.plot(np.arange(1, n + 1), running_mean, label="Running mean of A - B")
plt.axhline(0.04, linestyle="--", label="True treatment effect = 0.04")
plt.xlabel("Number of observations")
plt.ylabel("Cumulative average")
plt.title("Law of Large Numbers in the A/B Test")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Bootstrap Standard Errors
A point estimate by itself does not tell us how precise the estimated treatment effect is. To measure uncertainty, I use the bootstrap. The basic idea is to repeatedly resample with replacement from the observed data in each group, recompute the estimated treatment effect each time, and then use the spread of those bootstrap estimates to approximate the standard error.
I generate 1,000 bootstrap replications. In each replication, I sample 1,000 observations with replacement from group A and 1,000 observations with replacement from group B, then calculate the difference in sample means. The standard deviation of these bootstrap estimates is the bootstrap standard error.

n_boot = 1000
boot_thetas = np.empty(n_boot)

for i in range(n_boot):
    A_boot = np.random.choice(A, size=n, replace=True)
    B_boot = np.random.choice(B, size=n, replace=True)
    boot_thetas[i] = A_boot.mean() - B_boot.mean()

boot_se = boot_thetas.std(ddof=1)

analytic_se = np.sqrt(A.mean() * (1 - A.mean()) / n + B.mean() * (1 - B.mean()) / n)

ci_lower = theta_hat - 1.96 * boot_se
ci_upper = theta_hat + 1.96 * boot_se

bootstrap_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": ["Estimated treatment effect", "Bootstrap SE", "Analytical SE", "95% CI lower", "95% CI upper"],
    "Value": [theta_hat, boot_se, analytic_se, ci_lower, ci_upper]
})

text:
The Central Limit Theorem
The Central Limit Theorem explains why Normal-based statistical inference works so well in large samples. Even when the original data are not Normally distributed, the sampling distribution of the sample mean tends to become approximately Normal as the sample size gets larger. In this A/B test, the individual outcomes are Bernoulli, so the raw data are highly discrete. However, the estimated treatment effect can still have an approximately bell-shaped sampling distribution when the sample size is sufficiently large.
To illustrate this, I repeatedly simulate the estimated treatment effect at several different sample sizes. For each sample size, I generate many independent A/B tests, compute the difference in sample means, and then examine the distribution of those estimates.

sample_sizes = [25, 50, 100, 500]
n_sim = 1000

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
axes = axes.flatten()

for ax, sample_n in zip(axes, sample_sizes):
    theta_hats_sim = np.empty(n_sim)
    
    for i in range(n_sim):
        A_sim = np.random.binomial(1, pi_A, sample_n)
        B_sim = np.random.binomial(1, pi_B, sample_n)
        theta_hats_sim[i] = A_sim.mean() - B_sim.mean()
    
    ax.hist(theta_hats_sim, bins=30, edgecolor="black")
    ax.axvline(0.04, linestyle="--")
    ax.set_title(f"n = {sample_n}")
    ax.set_xlabel("Estimated treatment effect")
    ax.set_ylabel("Frequency")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Hypothesis Testing
A hypothesis test asks whether the observed difference in sign-up rates is large enough that it would be unlikely to occur just by random chance. In this A/B test, the null hypothesis is that the two CTAs perform equally well, while the alternative hypothesis is that they have different conversion rates:
\[
H_0: \theta = 0
\]
\[
H_1: \theta \neq 0
\]
Using the estimated treatment effect and its standard error, I compute a z-statistic. Under the null hypothesis, this statistic is approximately Standard Normal in large samples, which allows me to calculate a two-sided p-value.

z_stat = theta_hat / analytic_se
p_value = 2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(abs(z_stat)))

hypothesis_results = pd.DataFrame({

The T-Test as a Regression
The difference in means from an A/B test can also be written as a regression. To do this, I stack the two groups together into one dataset and create a treatment indicator equal to 1 for CTA A and 0 for CTA B. I then run the following regression:
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i
\]
where \(Y_i\) is the sign-up outcome and \(D_i\) indicates whether the visitor saw CTA A. In this setup, the intercept \(\beta_0\) is the mean outcome for group B, and the coefficient \(\beta_1\) is the difference in mean outcomes between group A and group B. That means the regression coefficient on the treatment indicator should match the estimated treatment effect from the A/B test.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Problem with Peeking
One important problem in experimentation is peeking at the data too often. Suppose the true conversion rates are actually the same, so there is no real treatment effect. If I run a hypothesis test only once at the end of the experiment, the probability of a false positive is about 5% when I use a 5% significance level. But if I repeatedly check the results during the experiment and stop as soon as I see significance, the overall false positive rate becomes much larger.
To demonstrate this, I simulate many experiments under the null hypothesis where both CTAs have the same sign-up probability of 0.20. In each experiment, I check for significance after every 100 observations per group, up to 1,000 observations per group. If any of those interim tests is significant at the 5% level, I count the experiment as producing a false positive.

np.random.seed(123)

pi_null = 0.20
n_total = 1000
checkpoints = np.arange(100, n_total + 1, 100)
n_experiments = 10000

false_positive_any = 0

for _ in range(n_experiments):
    A_null = np.random.binomial(1, pi_null, n_total)
    B_null = np.random.binomial(1, pi_null, n_total)
    
    rejected = False
    
    for m in checkpoints:
        A_m = A_null[:m]
        B_m = B_null[:m]
        
        theta_hat_m = A_m.mean() - B_m.mean()
        se_m = np.sqrt(A_m.mean() * (1 - A_m.mean()) / m + B_m.mean() * (1 - B_m.mean()) / m)
        
        if se_m > 0:
            z_m = theta_hat_m / se_m
            p_m = 2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(abs(z_m)))
            
            if p_m < 0.05:
                rejected = True
                break
    
    if rejected:
        false_positive_any += 1

false_positive_rate = false_positive_any / n_experiments

peeking_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": ["Nominal significance level", "False positive rate with repeated peeking"],
    "Value": [0.05, false_positive_rate]
})

If researchers want to monitor results during the experiment, they usually need special sequential testing methods rather than ordinary repeated hypothesis tests.

title: Does Blueprinty’s Software Help Firms Get More Patents?
text:
Blueprinty is a software company that helps engineering firms prepare and submit patent applications. The main business question in this post is whether firms that use Blueprinty’s software tend to receive more patents than firms that do not use it.
This question is important for Blueprinty’s marketing team because the company wants to support the claim that its software helps customers become more successful in the patent application process. However, this claim is not simple to evaluate. The firms that choose to use Blueprinty are not randomly selected. They may differ from non-customers in age, region, size, or other characteristics that also affect patent counts.
In this analysis, I use data from 1,500 mature engineering firms. The outcome variable is the number of patents each firm received over the last five years. The key explanatory variable is whether the firm is a Blueprinty customer. I first explore the raw differences between customers and non-customers, then estimate a Poisson regression model using maximum likelihood estimation. Because the data are observational, the results should be interpreted as evidence of an association rather than definitive causal proof.

section: A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
text:
A Simple Poisson Model via Maximum Likelihood
The outcome variable in this project is the number of patents awarded to each firm over the last five years. Since this variable is a non-negative count, a Poisson distribution is a natural starting point. A normal model would be less appropriate because it can predict negative values and does not directly represent count data.
For a single observation, the Poisson probability mass function is:
\[
f(y_i \mid \lambda) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{y_i}}{y_i!}
\]
If the observations are independent, the joint likelihood for all firms is:
\[
L(\lambda) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{y_i}}{y_i!}
\]
Taking logs gives the log-likelihood:
\[
\ell(\lambda) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[-\lambda + y_i \log(\lambda) - \log(y_i!)\right]
\]
This simple model assumes that all firms have the same expected number of patents. That is clearly a strong assumption, but it is a useful first step because it shows how maximum likelihood estimation works before adding firm-level predictors.

from scipy.optimize import minimize
from scipy.special import gammaln

y = blueprinty["patents"].to_numpy()

def poisson_loglik(lambda_value, y):
    if lambda_value <= 0:
        return -np.inf
    
    return np.sum(-lambda_value + y * np.log(lambda_value) - gammaln(y + 1))

def negative_poisson_loglik(lambda_array, y):
    lambda_value = lambda_array[0]
    return -poisson_loglik(lambda_value, y)

The function above returns the Poisson log-likelihood for a given value of \(\lambda\). Since numerical optimizers usually minimize functions, I also define the negative log-likelihood.









The log-likelihood curve has a clear maximum. The value of \(\lambda\) at this maximum is the maximum likelihood estimate.

simple_result = minimize(
    negative_poisson_loglik,
    x0=np.array([y.mean()]),
    args=(y,),
    method="BFGS"
)

lambda_mle = simple_result.x[0]
sample_mean = y.mean()

Poisson Regression
The simple Poisson model estimated one common patent rate for all firms. That is useful for showing the basic MLE idea, but it is too simple for the real business question. Blueprinty customers and non-customers may differ in firm age and region, so the next model allows the expected patent count to depend on firm characteristics.
For firm \(i\), I model the patent count as:
\[
Y_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i)
\]
and use a log link:
\[
\lambda_i = \exp(X_i \beta)
\]
The exponential function is important because it keeps the predicted patent count positive. In this model, \(X_i\) includes an intercept, customer status, firm age, firm age squared, and region indicators.

import statsmodels.api as sm

X = pd.get_dummies(
    blueprinty[["iscustomer", "age", "region"]],
    columns=["region"],

    dtype=float
)

X_np = X.to_numpy()

The Poisson regression log-likelihood is:
\[
\ell(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left[-\exp(X_i\beta) + y_i X_i\beta - \log(y_i!)\right]
\]
I estimate the model by minimizing the negative log-likelihood.

def poisson_reg_loglik(beta, X, y):
    xb = X @ beta
    lam = np.exp(xb)
    return np.sum(-lam + y * xb - gammaln(y + 1))

def negative_poisson_reg_loglik(beta, X, y):
    return -poisson_reg_loglik(beta, X, y)

initial_beta = np.zeros(X_np.shape[1])

    x0=initial_beta,
    args=(X_np, y),

)

title: Does Blueprinty’s Software Help Firms Get More Patents?
text:
Conclusion
This analysis used Poisson regression to study whether Blueprinty customers tend to receive more patents than non-customers. Since patent counts are non-negative count data, the Poisson model is a reasonable starting point. I first estimated a simple Poisson model using maximum likelihood, then extended the model to include customer status, firm age, age squared, and region controls.
The manual MLE estimates matched the standard GLM results, which confirms that the likelihood function was implemented correctly. The main result is that Blueprinty customer status has a positive association with expected patent counts. In practical terms, the counterfactual prediction suggests that firms are expected to receive more patents when they are treated as Blueprinty customers, holding age and region constant.
Overall, the findings are favorable for Blueprinty, but they should not be overstated. The model shows a strong association, not definitive causal proof. A better future study would use stronger causal evidence, such as before-and-after data, a randomized pilot, or more detailed controls for firm size, research spending, and prior patent activity.

text:
Suppose I manage a website with a landing page that invites visitors to sign up for a newsletter. I want to know whether the wording of the call to action affects whether visitors subscribe. In this experiment, CTA A says “Sign up for our newsletter here!” while CTA B says “Stay up to date by signing up!” Visitors are randomly assigned to see one of the two versions, and I compare the sign-up rates between the groups.
This is a standard A/B test. The goal is to estimate whether one version of the message leads to a higher conversion rate than the other. More broadly, this example provides a useful setting for understanding several key ideas in frequentist statistics, including simulation, the law of large numbers, the bootstrap, hypothesis testing, and the risks of repeated peeking at the data.

Suppose I manage a website with a landing page that invites visitors to sign up for a newsletter. I want to know whether the wording of the call to action affects whether visitors subscribe. In this experiment, CTA A says “Sign up for our newsletter here!” while CTA B says “Stay up to date by signing up!” Visitors are randomly assigned to see one of the two versions, and I compare the sign-up rates between the groups.
This is a standard A/B test. The goal is to estimate whether one version of the message leads to a higher conversion rate than the other. More broadly, this example provides a useful setting for understanding several key ideas in frequentist statistics, including simulation, the law of large numbers, the bootstrap, hypothesis testing, and the risks of repeated peeking at the data.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
section: The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
text:
The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
Each visitor either signs up for the newsletter or does not, so the outcome for each person is binary. Because of this, each observation can be modeled as a Bernoulli random variable with a success probability equal to the probability of signing up.
Let \(\pi_A\) represent the probability of signing up under CTA A, and let \(\pi_B\) represent the probability of signing up under CTA B. The main parameter of interest is the difference in conversion rates:
\[
\theta = \pi_A - \pi_B
\]
In the sample, I estimate this quantity using the difference in observed sign-up proportions:
\[
\hat{\theta} = \bar{X}_A - \bar{X}_B
\]
Since the outcome is either 0 or 1, the sample mean in each group is just the proportion of visitors who signed up. This makes the difference in sample means a natural estimator for the treatment effect in this A/B test.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Simulating Data
In a real A/B test, the true conversion rates would be unknown. However, simulation is useful because it allows me to study how the estimator behaves when the true values are known. For this exercise, I assume that the sign-up probability under CTA A is \(\pi_A = 0.22\) and the sign-up probability under CTA B is \(\pi_B = 0.18\). This means the true treatment effect is:
\[
\theta = 0.22 - 0.18 = 0.04
\]
Using these values, I simulate 1,000 visitors in each group and compare the observed conversion rates.

text:
The Law of Large Numbers
The Law of Large Numbers says that as the sample size grows, the sample average gets closer to the true population average. In this A/B test, that means the estimated treatment effect should move closer to the true difference in conversion rates as more observations are included. With only a few observations, the estimate can fluctuate a lot, but with a larger sample it becomes more stable.
To illustrate this, I compute the element-wise differences between the simulated outcomes in group A and group B, then calculate the cumulative average of those differences. If the Law of Large Numbers is working as expected, the running mean should gradually settle near the true treatment effect of 0.04.

diffs = A - B
running_mean = np.cumsum(diffs) / np.arange(1, n + 1)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.plot(np.arange(1, n + 1), running_mean, label="Running mean of A - B")
plt.axhline(0.04, linestyle="--", label="True treatment effect = 0.04")
plt.xlabel("Number of observations")
plt.ylabel("Cumulative average")
plt.title("Law of Large Numbers in the A/B Test")

text:
Bootstrap Standard Errors
A point estimate by itself does not tell us how precise the estimated treatment effect is. To measure uncertainty, I use the bootstrap. The basic idea is to repeatedly resample with replacement from the observed data in each group, recompute the estimated treatment effect each time, and then use the spread of those bootstrap estimates to approximate the standard error.
I generate 1,000 bootstrap replications. In each replication, I sample 1,000 observations with replacement from group A and 1,000 observations with replacement from group B, then calculate the difference in sample means. The standard deviation of these bootstrap estimates is the bootstrap standard error.

n_boot = 1000
boot_thetas = np.empty(n_boot)

for i in range(n_boot):
    A_boot = np.random.choice(A, size=n, replace=True)
    B_boot = np.random.choice(B, size=n, replace=True)
    boot_thetas[i] = A_boot.mean() - B_boot.mean()

boot_se = boot_thetas.std(ddof=1)

analytic_se = np.sqrt(A.mean() * (1 - A.mean()) / n + B.mean() * (1 - B.mean()) / n)

ci_lower = theta_hat - 1.96 * boot_se
ci_upper = theta_hat + 1.96 * boot_se

bootstrap_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": ["Estimated treatment effect", "Bootstrap SE", "Analytical SE", "95% CI lower", "95% CI upper"],
    "Value": [theta_hat, boot_se, analytic_se, ci_lower, ci_upper]

The Central Limit Theorem
The Central Limit Theorem explains why Normal-based statistical inference works so well in large samples. Even when the original data are not Normally distributed, the sampling distribution of the sample mean tends to become approximately Normal as the sample size gets larger. In this A/B test, the individual outcomes are Bernoulli, so the raw data are highly discrete. However, the estimated treatment effect can still have an approximately bell-shaped sampling distribution when the sample size is sufficiently large.
To illustrate this, I repeatedly simulate the estimated treatment effect at several different sample sizes. For each sample size, I generate many independent A/B tests, compute the difference in sample means, and then examine the distribution of those estimates.

sample_sizes = [25, 50, 100, 500]

Hypothesis Testing
A hypothesis test asks whether the observed difference in sign-up rates is large enough that it would be unlikely to occur just by random chance. In this A/B test, the null hypothesis is that the two CTAs perform equally well, while the alternative hypothesis is that they have different conversion rates:
\[
H_0: \theta = 0
\]
\[
H_1: \theta \neq 0
\]
Using the estimated treatment effect and its standard error, I compute a z-statistic. Under the null hypothesis, this statistic is approximately Standard Normal in large samples, which allows me to calculate a two-sided p-value.

z_stat = theta_hat / analytic_se

text:
The T-Test as a Regression
The difference in means from an A/B test can also be written as a regression. To do this, I stack the two groups together into one dataset and create a treatment indicator equal to 1 for CTA A and 0 for CTA B. I then run the following regression:
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i
\]
where \(Y_i\) is the sign-up outcome and \(D_i\) indicates whether the visitor saw CTA A. In this setup, the intercept \(\beta_0\) is the mean outcome for group B, and the coefficient \(\beta_1\) is the difference in mean outcomes between group A and group B. That means the regression coefficient on the treatment indicator should match the estimated treatment effect from the A/B test.

import statsmodels.api as sm

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Problem with Peeking
One important problem in experimentation is peeking at the data too often. Suppose the true conversion rates are actually the same, so there is no real treatment effect. If I run a hypothesis test only once at the end of the experiment, the probability of a false positive is about 5% when I use a 5% significance level. But if I repeatedly check the results during the experiment and stop as soon as I see significance, the overall false positive rate becomes much larger.
To demonstrate this, I simulate many experiments under the null hypothesis where both CTAs have the same sign-up probability of 0.20. In each experiment, I check for significance after every 100 observations per group, up to 1,000 observations per group. If any of those interim tests is significant at the 5% level, I count the experiment as producing a false positive.

np.random.seed(123)

pi_null = 0.20
n_total = 1000
checkpoints = np.arange(100, n_total + 1, 100)
n_experiments = 10000

false_positive_any = 0

for _ in range(n_experiments):
    A_null = np.random.binomial(1, pi_null, n_total)
    B_null = np.random.binomial(1, pi_null, n_total)
    
    rejected = False
    
    for m in checkpoints:
        A_m = A_null[:m]
        B_m = B_null[:m]
        
        theta_hat_m = A_m.mean() - B_m.mean()
        se_m = np.sqrt(A_m.mean() * (1 - A_m.mean()) / m + B_m.mean() * (1 - B_m.mean()) / m)
        
        if se_m > 0:
            z_m = theta_hat_m / se_m
            p_m = 2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(abs(z_m)))
            
            if p_m < 0.05:
                rejected = True
                break
    
    if rejected:
        false_positive_any += 1

false_positive_rate = false_positive_any / n_experiments

peeking_results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": ["Nominal significance level", "False positive rate with repeated peeking"],
    "Value": [0.05, false_positive_rate]
})

The simulation shows that repeated peeking makes false positives more likely. Even when there is no true difference between the two CTAs, checking the data over and over again creates more opportunities to incorrectly reject the null hypothesis. This is why classical hypothesis testing assumes that the testing plan is fixed in advance. If researchers want to monitor results during the experiment, they usually need special sequential testing methods rather than ordinary repeated hypothesis tests.

text:
In this post, I look at a simple A/B test for a call-to-action (CTA) on a website. The idea is to see which version of the CTA gets more people to sign up.
On the homepage, visitors will see one of two different messages. For example, one version might say “Sign up for our newsletter here!” while the other might say “Stay up to date by signing up!”. Even though they are similar, small differences in wording might affect how users respond.
An A/B test works by randomly assigning users to one of the two versions. Then we compare how many people sign up in each group. By comparing these results, we can get a sense of which CTA performs better.ii

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
section: The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
text:
The A/B Test as a Statistical Problem
To think about this A/B test statistically, I treat each user outcome as binary: either the person signs up or does not sign up. Because of that, it makes sense to model each outcome with a Bernoulli distribution.
The two CTA versions may lead to different sign-up rates, so I use (p_A) for the probability of signing up under CTA A and (p_B) for the probability of signing up under CTA B).
What I care about most is the difference between these two probabilities, which I can write as ( = p_A - p_B ). If this difference is positive, then CTA A performs better. If it is negative, then CTA B performs better.
In practice, I do not know the true values of (p_A) and (p_B), so I estimate them using the sample proportions from the data.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Simulating Data
In a real A/B test, we would not actually know the true values of (p_A) and (p_B). But for this simulation, I set them manually so I can see how the estimator behaves when the true difference is known.
Here, I let (p_A = 0.22) and (p_B = 0.18), so the true difference is ( = 0.04 ). Then I simulate outcomes for users in each group using a Bernoulli model.
By running the simulation many times, I can see how much the estimated difference changes from sample to sample, which helps show the variability in the estimates.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Law of Large Numbers
The Law of Large Numbers says that as the sample size increases, the sample average will get closer to the true value. In this context, it means that as we collect more data from the A/B test, our estimate of the difference between the two CTAs should become more stable.
At the beginning, when the sample size is small, the estimated difference can vary a lot due to randomness. But as we include more observations, the estimate should settle down and get closer to the true difference of 0.04.
This helps explain why larger sample sizes are important in A/B testing. With more data, we can be more confident that our estimate reflects the true effect rather than random variation.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Bootstrap Standard Errors
After getting an estimate for the difference between the two CTAs, the next question is how precise this estimate is. In other words, we want to know how much this estimate might change if we repeated the experiment.
To measure this, I use the bootstrap method. The basic idea is to repeatedly resample from the observed data and recompute the estimate each time. This allows me to approximate how much the estimate varies without relying on a closed-form formula.
In this case, I take the simulated data from the previous section and draw bootstrap samples (with replacement) from both groups. For each bootstrap sample, I compute the difference in means between CTA A and CTA B. Repeating this process many times gives a collection of estimated differences.
The variability of these estimates can be summarized by their standard deviation, which serves as the bootstrap standard error.
For comparison, the analytical standard error for the difference in proportions is given by:
\[
SE(\hat{\theta}) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_A (1 - \hat{p}_A)}{n_A} + \frac{\hat{p}_B (1 - \hat{p}_B)}{n_B}}
\]
Here, ( _A ) and ( _B ) are the sample proportions, and ( n_A ) and ( n_B ) are the sample sizes in each group.
I compare the bootstrap standard error with this analytical formula to see how close they are. If they are similar, it gives more confidence that the bootstrap approach is working as expected.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Central Limit Theorem
The Central Limit Theorem says that as the sample size increases, the distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately normal, even if the original data is not normally distributed.
In this case, I look at the distribution of the estimated difference in means for different sample sizes. When the sample size is small, the distribution looks more irregular and can be somewhat skewed. But as the sample size increases, the distribution becomes more symmetric and bell-shaped.
This shows that for larger samples, it is reasonable to treat the sampling distribution as approximately normal. This is useful because it allows us to use standard statistical tools that rely on normality.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
Hypothesis Testing
Now that we have an estimate and its standard error, we can use them to perform a hypothesis test.
The main idea is to check whether the observed difference could reasonably happen if there were actually no difference between the two CTAs. So I start with a null hypothesis that ( = 0 ).
To do this, I standardize the estimate using its standard error. This gives the test statistic:
\[
z = \frac{\hat{\theta} - 0}{SE(\hat{\theta})}
\]
This tells us how far the estimated difference is from 0 in terms of standard errors. If this value is large in magnitude, it suggests that the observed difference is unlikely to be due to random chance.
Since the sample size is large, the sampling distribution is approximately normal, so I can use the standard normal distribution to compute a p-value. This helps decide whether there is enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The T-Test as a Regression
It turns out that the two-sample test we used earlier can also be written as a simple regression. This provides another way to understand the same problem.
To set this up, I combine the data from both groups into a single dataset. The outcome variable (Y_i) indicates whether a user signed up (1) or not (0), and the variable (D_i) indicates which CTA the user saw (1 for A, 0 for B).
The regression model is:
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \varepsilon_i
\]
In this model, ( _0 ) represents the average outcome for group B, while ( _1 ) captures the difference between group A and group B. So ( _1 ) corresponds directly to the difference in sign-up rates that we have been estimating throughout the analysis.
This shows that the regression approach and the two-sample test are closely related. They give the same estimate for the difference, but the regression framework is more flexible and can be extended to more complex settings.

title: A/B Testing a Call to Action
text:
The Problem with Peeking
In practice, it can be tempting to check the results of an experiment early and stop as soon as we see a significant result. However, this can lead to incorrect conclusions.
The issue is that each time we look at the data and run a hypothesis test, there is a chance of getting a false positive. Even if the null hypothesis is true, a single test at the 5% level has a small probability of incorrectly rejecting it. But if we repeatedly check the results, these probabilities start to add up.
To see this more clearly, I simulate a situation where there is actually no difference between the two CTAs. Then I repeatedly check for significance as more data is added. Even though the null hypothesis is true, I often find at least one “significant” result just by chance.
This shows that peeking inflates the false positive rate. In other words, it makes us more likely to incorrectly conclude that there is a difference when there is none. This is why it is important to decide on a sample size in advance and avoid checking results too frequently during an experiment.
